strengths: The core architectural idea—decoupling modality-specific conditioning pathways (self-attention for vision, AdaLN for proprioception/task conditions, cross-attention for tactile)—is a clean and well-motivated design choice, validated by ablations (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds/DECO.p) that isolate the benefit of the decoupled fusion mechanism from simply adding tactile embeddings.

The plugin tactile adapter is genuinely parameter-efficient (7.97M trainable parameters vs. 83–91M total, an order of magnitude less than full fine-tuning) while achieving the largest reported gains on contact-rich tasks, which is a practically useful result for adapting pretrained visuomotor policies.

The paper contributes a new bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset (DECO-50) with active vision and dense tactile sensing (1062 contact points), which fills a documented gap relative to existing datasets (Table 9), and is collected on real hardware with meaningful scale (50 hours, ~8K successful trajectories).

Real-world evaluation is extensive by robotics-paper standards (>2000 rollouts across 4 tasks with per-object and per-stage breakdowns), and the analysis thoughtfully distinguishes tactile-relevant tasks (waste disposal, assembly) from tasks where vision/proprioception suffice (pick-and-place, material sorting), providing actionable insight rather than blanket claims.
Detailed appendices document data collection protocol, training hyperparameters, and per-object/per-stage results, aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single custom hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands and a bespoke active camera/teleop pipeline); there is no evaluation in simulation or on a second embodiment, so generalizability of the architectural claims beyond this specific setup is unverified.

Baselines are limited to ACT and Diffusion Policy (plus a naively tactile-concatenated DP.t); despite the related-work section citing several recent tactile-VLA/visuo-tactile works (e.g., Tactile-VLA, VTLA, ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy), none are used as empirical baselines, making it hard to judge whether DECO's decoupled fusion is actually superior to other modern fusion schemes rather than just superior to a simple concatenation baseline.

Reported success rates are based on small trial counts per condition (e.g., 20 or 80 trials) with no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or variance estimates, so it is difficult to assess the statistical reliability of relatively small performance gaps between methods (e.g., DECO vs. DP.t on several sub-tasks).

The dataset and task suite, while a useful contribution, remain modest in scale and diversity (4 scenarios, 28 sub-tasks) relative to the scale needed to support claims of general applicability to pretrained VLA models; the paper's own future-work section acknowledges long-horizon and larger-scale VLA integration is unaddressed.

The theoretical justification for the central hypothesis ("different modalities contribute differently to action generation, hence require different injection mechanisms") is asserted rather than analytically derived or tested against alternative pairings of mechanisms-to-modalities (e.g., cross-attention for proprioception, AdaLN for tactile), so the specific mechanism-modality assignment in DECO is empirically supported but not theoretically motivated.

No explicit statement on code/dataset release plans, and the specialized teleoperation/hardware requirements (custom active camera, Vision Pro-based retargeting, specific dexterous hands) make exact reproduction by other groups challenging even if the dataset itself were released.

strengths: Extensive real-world validation: over 2,000 robot rollouts across 4 tasks (pick-and-place, material sorting, waste disposal, assembly) with detailed per-object breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, which is unusually thorough for a real-robot manipulation paper.

Release of DECO-50, a genuinely useful bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision (50+ hours, ~8K trajectories, 28 sub-tasks) that fills a documented gap in existing bimanual/tactile datasets (Table 11 comparison is informative).

Well-designed, informative ablations: the coupled-vs-decoupled tactile injection comparison (DECO vs DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p) and especially the pathway-swap experiment (Table 7, proprioception via cross-attention vs AdaLN) provide fairly convincing evidence that the specific modality-to-pathway assignment matters, not just the presence of separate pathways.

The plugin tactile adapter is a practically valuable contribution: it achieves performance close to full retraining (DECO.ds) while updating <10% of parameters, which is attractive for efficient adaptation of pretrained visuomotor policies to new sensing modalities.

Extensive supplementary simulation experiments across four independent public benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) show DECO is competitive with or exceeds several larger/pretrained VLA baselines despite substantially fewer parameters and no external pretraining, strengthening generality claims beyond the custom real-robot setup.
Reasonably detailed methodological and data-collection documentation (teleoperation setup, tactile sensor layout, training hyperparameters) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: AdaLN conditioning, joint self-attention, cross-attention for auxiliary modalities, and LoRA adapters are all well-established building blocks; the contribution is mainly their particular assignment to modalities, which is justified largely post-hoc/empirically (via the one swap ablation) rather than from a principled design argument.

Real-world baselines are limited to relatively simple/older methods (ACT, DP, and a naive-concatenation DP.t variant); no direct real-world comparison to more recent visuo-tactile fusion architectures discussed in related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, OmniVTLA), making it harder to assess whether DECO's decoupled design is actually superior to other tactile-fusion strategies, not just to naive concatenation.

Evaluation is confined to a single hardware platform, one dexterous hand, and one tactile sensor type (acknowledged as a limitation), so claims about the generality of the decoupled paradigm and the tactile adapter's transferability remain unverified across embodiments/sensor modalities beyond the additional simulation benchmarks.

Per-condition real-world trial counts are often small (e.g., 10–20 trials per object), yielding wide confidence intervals in several tables; some reported gains (e.g., in Task 1, or certain Task 2 objects) may not be statistically distinguishable between methods despite being described as improvements.
No indication of multiple training seeds/runs for the main real-world comparisons, so variance due to training stochasticity is not quantified, which is relevant given the modest sample sizes.

The pathway-swap ablation (Table 7) explores only one alternative permutation (swapping tactile and proprioception pathways) rather than a more complete combinatorial ablation (e.g., vision via AdaLN, tactile via self-attention, etc.), limiting how strongly the results generalize to support the broader claim that the specific decoupled design is optimal versus merely one reasonable choice among many.

strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated architectural principle—decoupling modality-specific conditioning pathways (self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception/task-level conditions, cross-attention for tactile)—and provides a clear ablation (Table 7, pathway-swap experiment) that convincingly demonstrates the pathway assignment is crucial, with dramatic drops (e.g., 0/40 vs 29/40 on Stage 3) when pathways are swapped.

Extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across 4 diverse bimanual dexterous tasks (pick-and-place, dynamic sorting, contact-rich waste disposal, and precision assembly), with per-object breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, lending good statistical rigor to the real-robot claims.

The plugin tactile adapter is a practically valuable contribution: it achieves performance comparable to full retraining (DECO.ds) while updating <10% of parameters (7.97M vs 89.41M), a meaningful demonstration of parameter-efficient multimodal adaptation for pretrained visuomotor policies.

DECO-50 fills a genuine gap in the literature (bimanual + dexterous + tactile + active vision, real robot) as shown by the thorough dataset comparison table, and is accompanied by detailed collection/hardware documentation (tactile pad layout, teleoperation setup) supporting reproducibility.

The supplementary simulation results across four independent benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) with comparisons to strong published baselines substantially strengthen generality claims beyond the single real-world hardware platform, and the ResNet-18 vs ResNet-34 ablation controls for a natural confound versus baselines using ResNet-18.

Detailed failure-mode analysis (e.g., timeout vs. slip breakdown in UniVTAC, per-stage analysis in waste disposal/assembly) provides good qualitative insight into why and where tactile signal helps or doesn't.
weaknesses: The core empirical claims rest on a single hardware embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) and a single tactile sensor type; while acknowledged as a limitation, this restricts confidence that the decoupled-pathway design generalizes to other tactile sensor characteristics (e.g., shear-sensitive sensors) or hand morphologies.

Some real-world success-rate differences, especially in Task 1 and parts of Task 2, are based on relatively small per-object trial counts (10-20 trials), leading to wide/overlapping confidence intervals, so several individual comparisons are not clearly statistically significant even though aggregate trends are.

The justification for the specific modality-to-pathway mapping is largely empirical/post hoc (motivated by the swap ablation) rather than derived from a principled theory of what modality property should dictate the pathway, leaving open whether the assignment used is optimal versus merely one workable configuration.
The DECO.cs (coupled tactile fusion) ablation is only tested on 2 object pairs in the assembly task, a fairly narrow basis for the paper's central 'decoupling helps' claim relative to naive fusion.

The extensive supplementary simulation benchmarking compares against numbers taken from other papers under possibly different training budgets/protocols (self-reported baselines), which weakens direct comparison conclusions and is not deeply discussed as a caveat.

Presentation could be improved: some architectural details (e.g., precise interaction between the adapter and LoRA within the same forward pass) are terse in the main text and require cross-referencing the appendix for full clarity.
